newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil panel set to vote tonight on telecoms law.
newsitem.headline: Brazil panel set to vote tonight on telecoms law.

text.p: Congressmen are scrambling to make last minute changes in a bill regulating Brazil's telecoms sector ahead of a key vote tonight in a lower house committee, officials said.

"Deputies will be speaking to each other today to reach an accord. We expect they will vote tonight," said a spokeswoman for Deputy Alberto Goldman, the legislator charged with drafting the General Telecommunications Law.
The 30-member Special Telecommunications Committee is slated to begin taking up the issue at 1900 local/1800 EDT.
If approved by 16 votes, the bill will go to the full Chamber of Deputies on Friday for a possible vote and then to the Senate. The government hopes the bill to win final approval next month.
But approval by the committee, where the bulk of discussion on the legislation will have occurred, is key and would signal its likely passage in the full chamber.

The law, which is anxiously awaited by financial markets and telecoms operators worldwide, has been delayed in committee because lawmakers have been unable to decide what the level of participation foreign capital should be allowed in new private Brazilian telecoms operators.
"That is the main sticking point," a congressional source said, adding party leaders in the committee have reached a tentative accord but have yet to convince Goldman to alter his bill.

Goldman's text would leave it up to the president to set a limit on foreign participation in Brazilian telecoms. But party leaders last week said they had agreed to allow foreigners minimum 49 percent and maximum 100 percent stakes.
The source said lawmakers are likely to reach an agreement with Goldman during informal discussions today so he may present amendments to his bill tonight.
After two failed attempts to vote on the bill last week, lawmakers agreed to postpone voting until this week.
The general telecoms law also would set the rules for a newly private telecoms sector after years of state control and authorize the privatization of the federal Telebras
The government hopes to privatize Telebras starting late this year or early in 1998, beginning with its two largest units Telesp and long-distance monopoly Embratel.
The new telecoms law also would create a regulatory watchdog for the sector called the National Telecommunications Agency, or Antel.
The body would have the power to prevent investors or groups from dominating the industry and would have its own budget to ensure autonomy.
The law also would:
* Establish rules for granting concessions, licenses and authorizations to operate telecom services in Brazil;
* Ensure competition in the sector;
* Create a fund to guarantee all Brazilians access to the country's telecoms system;
* And encourage research and development of new technology in the sector.
((--Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 2485413))
